summary: EVPN multihoming must keep traffic from looping back to a device that already sent it, a job called split-horizon filtering. Different tunnel types, such as overlay tunnels versus MPLS or Segment Routing, use different methods. This RFC extends BGP EVPN signalling so networks mixing these tunnel types can coordinate the filtering.

eli5.summary: If you shout a message across the room, it should not echo right back to you. This helps network devices avoid sending your own message back to you when several paths exist.

subtitle: Lets EVPN operators choose which loop-prevention method multihomed devices use, and tells every peer about the choice.

tldr.problem: When a customer device is attached to several provider edge devices, a broadcast frame must not be sent back to the segment it came from. Two filtering methods exist, ESI Label and local bias, but older specifications tied each method to a tunnel type and gave operators no choice, even for tunnels that can do both.
tldr.mechanism: The two high-order bits of the Flags octet in the ESI Label extended community become a Split-Horizon Type (SHT) field. Each edge device uses it in its A-D per ES route to say which method it intends to use, and everyone falls back to the default if the advertisements disagree.
tldr.outcome: Operators can pick the method for tunnels such as MPLSoUDP, MPLSoGRE, Geneve and SRv6, while devices that only implement RFC 7432 or RFC 8365 keep working because the default value 00 means the old behavior.

facts.label: SHT field
facts.value: 2 bits (bits 6 and 7 of the Flags octet)

today: RFC 9746 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2025 that updates RFC 7432 and RFC 8365. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Why Split Horizon Needs a Choice
sections.content:
Split horizon is the EVPN multihoming rule that stops a Provider Edge (PE) device from sending a frame back to a multihomed Customer Edge (CE) device when that CE originated the frame. EVPN is used with several tunnel types: Network Virtualization Overlay (NVO) tunnels per RFC 8365, MPLS and SR-MPLS tunnels per RFC 7432, and SRv6 tunnels per RFC 9252.

Two procedures exist to prevent looped frames: the ESI Label-based procedure for MPLS or MPLS over X tunnels, and local bias for IP-based tunnels such as VXLAN. The problem is that some tunnels can carry either one, and the current specifications do not let operators choose. RFC 9746 updates RFC 7432 and RFC 8365 to add that choice.

The RFC does not change either filtering procedure itself. It only adds signaling and selection of which method the multihomed devices apply.
sections.eli5: A message should never bounce back to the one who sent it. There are two ways to check for that, and this RFC lets the network pick which one to use.

sections.title: Two Ways to Filter
sections.content:
With ESI Label filtering, the ingress device adds a label identifying the source Ethernet Segment (ESI) when it encapsulates a frame. The egress device checks that label before forwarding a multi-destination frame onto a local segment, and if the label matches that segment's ESI, the frame is dropped. This works for both All-Active and Single-Active multihoming, and for Single-Active it also helps avoid transient loops when the egress device becomes the Designated Forwarder (DF).

With local bias, the egress device looks at the source IP address in the tunnel header, which identifies the ingress device, and filters the frame on every local interface connected to a segment it shares with that ingress device. To make that work, the ingress device always replicates locally to all its directly attached segments, whatever the DF state. Local bias is not suitable for Single-Active multihoming, and it only works where the next hop does not change between devices attached to the same segment.

Some operators still prefer local bias because it simplifies encapsulation, uses fewer resources on the devices, and lets the ingress device forward locally, which reduces delay in reaching multihomed hosts.
sections.eli5: One way is putting a name sticker on every note so its writer can spot it. The other way is the room remembering who sits next to whom, so a note is never handed to the writer's own group.

sections.title: Which Tunnels Support What
sections.content:
The RFC sorts encapsulations into four groups: IP-based MPLS tunnels, MPLS and SR-MPLS tunnels, IP tunnels, and SRv6 tunnels. IP-based MPLS tunnels and SRv6 can support both methods. Plain MPLS and SR-MPLS support only ESI Label filtering. IP tunnels support local bias and may also support ESI Label filtering if their header can identify the source ESI. Encapsulations not in the table are out of scope.

Each encapsulation has a default split-horizon type. For Geneve the default depends on whether the Ethernet option with a Source ID TLV is negotiated. In the RFC's table, SRv6 is listed with ESI Label filtering as its default, because it behaves like it.
sections.eli5: Some tunnels only know one way to check. Others know both, and those are the ones where a choice makes sense.

sections.title: The Split-Horizon Type Field
sections.content:
Every EVPN device attached to an Ethernet Segment advertises an A-D per ES route that carries the ESI Label extended community. That community has a Flags octet. RFC 7432 defines the low-order bit as the Single-Active bit: 0 means All-Active and 1 means Single-Active. This RFC treats it as part of a new two-bit Multihoming Redundancy Mode field and uses the two high-order bits (bits 6 and 7) as the Split-Horizon Type (SHT).

The SHT values are 00 for the default method (backwards compatible with RFC 7432 and RFC 8365), 01 for local bias, 10 for ESI Label-based filtering, and 11 unassigned. An egress device that does not implement this RFC ignores the SHT bits, which is the same as reading them as 00.
sections.eli5: It is a tiny two-bit switch on each device's announcement. It says "use the usual way", "use local bias" or "use name stickers".

sections.title: Rules for Using the SHT
sections.content:
The SHT value is an intent, not necessarily what is actually used. The rules are:

  • An SHT of 01 or 10 MUST NOT be used with an encapsulation that supports only one method, and MAY be used with encapsulations that support both.
  • If the devices on the same segment advertise inconsistent SHT values for an EVI, all of them MUST revert to the RFC 8365 behavior and use the default from the table.
  • An SHT other than 00 MUST NOT be set when the Single-Active bit is set. A route with both set follows the treat-as-withdraw behavior of RFC 7606.
  • The SHT MUST be the same in every A-D per ES route a device advertises for a given segment and encapsulation.

For VXLAN (type 8), NVGRE (type 9), MPLS (type 10), or routes with no BGP Tunnel Encapsulation Extended Community, the SHT MUST be 00. Geneve (type 19) MAY use 01 or 10, and 10 is valid only if an Ethernet option TLV with a non-zero Source-ID is present. The ESI Label value may be zero when the SHT is 01, which saves allocating labels that local bias never uses.
sections.eli5: Everyone must agree before the fancy way is used. If even one device says something different, they all go back to the old default way.

sections.title: Old Devices and Multiple Encapsulations
sections.content:
A device keeps an administrative SHT (what it advertises) and an operational SHT (what it actually uses). If an upgraded device receives at least one A-D per ES route for the segment with SHT 00, it MUST revert its operational SHT to the default from the table. For example, if one peer sends 00 and another sends 01, the receiver uses the default. All devices with operational SHT 10 MUST advertise a valid, non-zero ESI Label.

If a device changes from local bias to the default because a non-upgraded device joined, and it had advertised a zero ESI Label, it MUST send an update with a valid non-zero label, unless all non-upgraded devices support only local bias.

A device that supports several encapsulations advertises only encapsulations that share a split-horizon method in the same route. If they all support only one method, the SHT MUST be 00. If they all support both, the SHT MAY be 01 or 10. If a segment needs different methods for different groups of route targets, a separate A-D per ES route (or group of routes) per method MUST be advertised, each with a distinct Route Distinguisher.
sections.eli5: If a new kid does not know the new rule, everybody quietly goes back to the old rule until the kid learns it.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registries
sections.content:
All security considerations of RFC 7432 apply. The new risk is misconfiguration of the SHT, which could produce forwarding behavior that differs from what was intended. Because a mismatch makes every device fall back to the default, an attacker changing the SHT on a single device should not cause traffic disruption as long as the value is valid, though forwarding behavior may change.

IANA created three registries: "EVPN ESI Label Extended Community Flags" (bits 6-7 assigned to the Split-Horizon Type), "Multihoming Redundancy Mode" (00 All-Active, 01 Single-Active), and "Split-Horizon Type" (00 Default, 01 Local Bias, 10 ESI Label-based filtering). New entries use the IETF Review procedure.
sections.eli5: If one device says something odd, the rest just use the safe default, so one troublemaker cannot easily break things.
